desc:
You are given an integer array nums and an integer k. You must perform exactly k operations. In one operation you pick any index i and replace nums[i] by -nums[i]. The same index may be picked in several operations.

Return the largest possible sum of the array after exactly k operations.

nums = [3, -1, 0, 2], k = 3          -> 6
nums = [2, -3, -1, 5, -4], k = 2     -> 13
nums = [1, 2], k = 3                 -> 1

In the first example flip -1 once; the two remaining operations flip the same element (for example 0) twice, so they change nothing.
hints: A flip helps only when it turns a negative number positive. Which negative numbers gain the most?
The most negative ones: flipping -9 gains 18, flipping -1 gains 2. Sort the array and flip from the smallest value upward.

After all negatives are flipped (or k runs out), leftover flips come in pairs that cancel. Only if an odd number remains you must lose by flipping once: do it on the element with the smallest absolute value, costing twice that value.
editorial: Sort the array ascending. Walk from the left: while the current value is negative and flips remain, flip it. Negative numbers farthest from zero come first, so each flip gains as much as possible.

If flips remain afterwards, all values are now non-negative. Flipping any element twice returns it to its value, so only the parity of the remaining flips matters. If it is even, nothing changes. If it is odd, exactly one flip has to be wasted, and the cheapest one is on the element with the smallest absolute value m (this includes a zero, which costs nothing): subtract 2 * m from the sum.
Note that the smallest absolute value must be taken after the flips, because a flipped element can become the smallest. Time is O(n log n) for the sort.
